div.p: This paper proposes an integrated duplication based Algorithm (IDSA) for improving the schedulability of precedence related real-time tasks with hard and soft deadlines on a set of heterogeneous network of workstations (NOWs). IDSA utilizes selective subtask duplication that enables some subtasks to have earlier start times, which results in an increased number of subtasks (and hence task sets) finishing before their deadlines, thereby increasing the Schedulability. Extensive theoretical analysis of the proposed IDSA scheme has been carried out. To that end, both the time and space complexity analysis of IDSA has been proved, in addition to its schedulability condition.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems are defined to be systems in which timely availability of results is critical, in addition to their correctness [37]. Based on the implications of allowable deadline misses, real-time tasks can be divided into two categories -hard tasks and soft tasks [37]. The consequence of a deadline miss of a hard real-time task can be prohibitively expensive whereas soft real-time task systems tolerate "some" deadline misses as long as they are within "acceptable" limits. It may very well be the case that the real-time application consists of a mix of hard and soft realtime tasks. Hence, it is intuitive to look at a common scheduling platform capable of supporting both these types of tasks [32 -34, 39]. One application that comes to mind is using Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) such as the Aerosonde robotic aircraft [38]. These UAVs are used to go to the epicenter of dangerous places such as earthquakes and hurricanes and then report the observed data back to the base. The operations performed by these vehicles have both kinds of tasks -hard real-time (command and control tasks), and soft real-time (handling and processing audio-visual information). Also, with the advent of cheap processors, it is not uncommon to have a set of heterogeneous processors with different speeds and configurations, communicating with each other and completing execution of an application. This has lead to the advent of a new class of computing systems called real-time heterogeneous multiprocessor systems [13, 14, 16, 17, 18 -20].

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: In [1], Liu and Layland propose the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and Rate Monotonic (RM) algorithms for executing real-time periodic tasks on a single processor. Papers [3,4] address the scheduling of real-time tasks on homogeneous multiprocessors. In other words, they assume that every real-time task takes the same execution time on any of the system processors. In our work, we assume a realtime task to have different execution time on different processors.

Real-time scheduling on heterogeneous multiprocessors has also been researched recently. Papers [5,6] extend the popular EDF algorithm for a set of heterogeneous multiprocessors. One of the limitations of this work is that it assumes independence between various subtasks, which is too naïve an assumption. In [7], Peng and Shin propose an optimal solution to the problem of scheduling periodic tasks on a set of heterogeneous processing nodes of a distributed real-time system. However, their algorithm is based on a branch-and-bound approach and its practical feasibility is yet to be established.

Papers [8,9] consider the scheduling of periodic tasks with precedence constraints. In [8], the authors propose an optimal algorithm for scheduling systems with precedence, periodicity and latency constraints. Spuri and Stankovic [9] extend the formal results of the real-time scheduling of precedence-constrained, unit time tasks to arbitrary timed tasks with preemption. However, both [8,9] assume that the real-time system comprises of a single processor.

The fault-tolerant aspect of real-time scheduling has been well researched in [10 -12]. Most of these schemes use the primary-backup approach in which each real-time task has two duplicate copies -a primary and a backup copy. The primary and backup copies are allocated to different processors. In case the primary copy fails, the backup copy is executed. Hence, the real-time task is duplicated for faulttolerance purposes. In contrast, our aim in employing duplication is to increase the success ratio of the real-time task set. The roots of our scheme can be found in [13,14]. However, both [13,14] do not consider real-time tasks.

The integrated scheduling of hard and soft real-time tasks on multiprocessors has been discussed in previous papers [16 -18]. However, these papers assume that each subtask has the same execution time on different processors. Hence, ___________________________________ 978-1-4244 -8679-3/11/$26.00 ©2011 IEEE these algorithms will not work for heterogeneous multiprocessor systems, something that our proposed algorithm is capable of.

div.head: III. TASK MODEL
div.p: In this research, it has been assumed that the real-time application consists of a mix of independent hard tasks and soft tasks, RT = {H, S}. Each hard periodic task can be further sub-divided into a set of subtasks, where each subtask has communication as well as precedence constraints with other subtasks. The application can be modeled as a set of DAGs [3], where each node corresponds to a subtask and each edge corresponds to a precedence relation between two subtasks.

According to a typical real-time task model [21], the period of a hard task (h a ) is assumed to be pd a . It has been assumed that one invocation (k) of all subtasks (st(i,j,k)) in a task needs to be executed every period. The deadline of the periodic task is assumed to be d a , and it is at the end of its period. The schedule is generated for a length equal to the plan period (pp), which is defined as the least common multiple of all task periods [21]. The worst case execution time array of a hard subtask is given by C(st(i,j,k),p k ).

Since, the subtask can have potentially different execution times on different processors; its execution time requirement is represented in the form of an array. The communication cost between two hard subtasks st(i,j,k) and st(i,l,k) of a task h a ∈H is given by c((st(i,j,k),st(i,l,k)). AP denotes the number of processors available to IDSA and CNP denotes the critical number of processors required for the initial cluster generation. The initial cluster generation is the number of initial clusters generated by the algorithms. It is equal to the number of passes though the code of IDSA.

The worst case execution time of a soft task task is given by the array C(s b ,p k ), where s b ∈S and p k ∈P. The deadline of a soft task s b ∈S is given by d b = Ω (rt-dag) + α, where Ω (rt-dag) is the critical path length of the DAG and α is a constant parameter selected uniformly from a specified range [min α, max α]. The communication cost between two soft tasks s b and s c is given by c(s b ,s c ), where s b , s c ∈S and b≠c. The set of predecessors of a soft task s b ∈S is depicted as Pred(s b ). The set of successors of a soft task s b ∈S is given by Succ(s b ).

A subtask is assumed to be non-preemptive. The underlying target architecture is assumed to be heterogeneous, with processors of different speeds and types. It is also assumed that an I/O coprocessor is available so that computation and communication can be performed concurrently. It is assumed that the duplicate subtasks are consistent with the original subtasks. The set of processors have been assumed to be dedicated. In other words, they are free unless a subtask has been scheduled to execute on them.

We assume that a set of processors are connected by a point-to-point network. A deadline driven protocol called the earliest-due-date-deadline (EDD-D) is used to schedule messages between the real-time subtasks [42]. When a subtask called the sender s wishes to send a message to subtask called the destination d, EDD-D sets up a channel s d. The set of messages in the system is represented by M = {m 1 , m 2 , m 3 … m n } and each message is characterized by its deadline, given by d(m i ), given m i ∈ M. Messages are scheduled to be transmitted on links between pair of processors. Each link can be represented as l d ∈L, where L is the set of links.

div.head: IV. MATHEMATICAL QUANTITIES FOR IDSA
div.p: The crux of IDSA is in the generation of subtask clusters based on the calculation of a set of mathematical quantities for each hard and soft task in the real-time application. The earliest start time of a subtask st(i,j,k) ∈ST(h i ), denoted by est(st(i,j,k)) is defined as the earliest time that the subtask can commence execution. Note that a subtask cannot start execution before its earliest start time. If a subtask and its predecessor subtask are assigned to the same processor, then the communication cost between them (if any) is assumed to be zero.

The earliest completion time of a subtask st(i,j,k) ∈ST(h a ) is denoted by ect(st(i,j,k)) and it is defined to be the earliest time that the particular subtask can finish execution on any one of the heterogeneous processors. The earliest completion time of a subtask is simply the sum of its earliest start time and its execution time on its favorite processor. The favorite processor of a subtask st(i,j,k) ∈ST(h a ), denoted by fp(st(i,j,k)) is defined to be the processor on which the subtask has the least completion time. However, a subtask may not have the shortest running time on its favorite processor. The favorite predecessor of a subtask st(i,j,k) ∈ST(h a ), denoted by fpred(st(i,j,k)) is defined as the processor p k ∈P that has the maximum value of earliest completion time plus the execution cost among all the predecessors of that particular subtask. The significance of the favorite predecessor is that if st(i,j,k) and fpred(st(i,j,k)) = st(i,b,k) are assigned to the same processor, then st(i,j,k) would have the least completion time. Hence, a subtasks' favorite predecessor is always the bottleneck for its completion. The latest allowable start time of a subtask st(i,j,k) ∈ST(h a ) is defined as the latest time that the subtask can start execution. It is denoted by last(st(i,j,k)). The latest available completion time of a subtask st(i,j,k) ∈ST(h a ), denoted by lact(st(i,j,k)) is defined as the latest time that the subtask can finish execution. The quantities last and lact are used to determine how critical two subtasks are to each other.

div.head: V. IDSA ALGORITHM STEPS
div.p: This section describes the working of our proposed scheduling algorithm. IDSA accepts as input the real-time application RT that consists of a mix of hard and soft tasks (i.e. S and H respectively). The application can be represented as a set of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) with the nodes representing the real-time subtasks and the edges between them representing the precedence relationship between the subtasks. The proposed algorithm consists of the following steps:

Step 1: First, the period of the first hard task and then subsequently, that of the other tasks is calculated. Then, the plan period is calculated by obtaining the least common multiple of all task periods.
Step 2: In this step, the DAG is traversed from top to bottom and the quantities est, ect, fpred, and fp are calculated for each subtask in the DAG.

Step 3: In this step the last and the lact are calculated for each subtask according to a bottom up traversal of the DAG. These quantities are used to find out if any two subtasks in a periodic task are critical to each other.

Step 4: In this step, a data structure called the queue is generated for each subtask in the periodic task. The queue consists of all subtasks arranged in a non-decreasing order of level. The significance of queue is that when the cluster generation takes place for each periodic task, the subtasks within a task are selected according to the order of the subtasks in the queue.

Step 5: In this step, the cluster generation takes place. The DAG is traversed in a bottom-up approach starting from the exit node. Here, an initial set of clusters is generated using available processors. The DAG is traversed bottom-up starting with the exit node. The aim is to try to generate clusters by following the favorite predecessor chain till the entry node is reached. If the fpred has already been assigned or if it is not critical, an unassigned predecessor having the lowest execution time on the current processor is selected. The significance of subtask criticality is that if two subtasks are not critical to each other, they can be assigned to different processors. Once a cluster is formed, the next cluster is built starting with the next unassigned element of the queue. This process continues recursively, till all the queue elements have been exhausted. Each cluster is then assigned to the first available fp of the header subtask of that cluster. For example, if fp 1 has already been assigned to another cluster, then fp 2 is chosen to accommodate the cluster. If fp 2 has also been assigned, then fp 3 is chosen and so on. T
Step 6: Steps 1 to 5 are repeated for all the periodic tasks in the application.
Step 7: In this step, the quantities est, ect, fp, fpred, last, lact are calculated for each soft task s b ∈S in the application.
These tasks are then assigned to suitable processors by following the cluster generation phase.

Step 8: If the number of available processors (AP) is greater than the number of processors required by the initial set of clusters (CNP), subtask duplication is carried out to increase the success ratio of the real-time application. A check is carried out to see if each subtask in a cluster is preceded by its fpred subtask. If this is not the case, then the tail of that particular cluster is replaced with its fpred chain till the entry node. The cut off tail is assigned to the next available fp of the last node of that tail. Duplication is carried out till all subtasks are preceded by their favorite predecessors or till there are no more processors remaining.

div.head: A. Time complexity:
div.p: Let the total number of DAGs in the real-time application = D. Now, D can be partitioned into dh and ds. All the DAGs in dh correspond to the hard real-time tasks in the application. Similarly, all the DAGs in ds correspond to the soft real-time tasks in the application. As each hard real-time task corresponds to a DAG, dh can be thought of as a set of DAGs dih such that dih = {d1h, d2h…….}. Using a similar logic, ds can also be thought of as a set of DAGs dis such that dis = {d1s, d2s……..}. Assuming that the following holds: nih = total number of hard subtasks in DAG dih and nis = total number of soft subtasks in DAG dis

div.head: 1) complexity due to soft subtasks:
div.p: First, we need to calculate the complexity for one specific DAG dis that has nis subtasks. The first step of RT-DBA involves calculating the values of est, ect, fpred, fprocm, p_e and queue. While calculating the est, for each node, all the predecessors need to be examined. Also, in the worst case, all edges need to be traversed. In the worst case, the number of predecessors will be equivalent to nis. therefore for nis, nodes the complexity for calculating est is O(nis2 + e). While calculating the fproc, for each node, all p processors need to be examined. Therefore, for nis nodes, the complexity is O(nis*p). While calculating the ect, all nodes need to be examined. Therefore, the complexity for this stage is O(nis).While calculating the value of p_e, for each node, nis nodes need to be examined in the worst case. Therefore, for nis nodes, the complexity is O(nis2). The formation of the queue involves arranging all nodes in increasing order of their p_e values. An algorithm such as quick sort can be used for this purpose. Therefore, the complexity of the queue formation stage is O(nis*log2*nis). While calculating the fpred, for each node, roughly nis predecessors need to be examined in the worst case. Therefore, for nis nodes, the complexity is O(nis2). On adding all the above, the complexity becomes O(nis2 + e + nis + nis*p + nis2 + e + nis*log2nis). For most practical DAGs and dense graphs, nis >> p and e is of the order of nis2. Hence, the complexity becomes O(nis2). The second step deals with the calculation of the quantities bst and bct. This involves a bottom-up traversal of the DAG. The complexity of this step is O(e). The next step involves the formation of the clusters. This is similar to a depth first search of the DAG and the complexity of this step is O(nis+e). For a connected graph, this is equivalent to O(e) in the worst case.

The complexity of the duplication stage is given by O(t* nis), where t is the number of subtasks not preceded by their fpred subtasks. In the worst case, all the subtasks are duplicated. In other words, t = nis. Hence, the complexity becomes O(nis2). The next stage is the cluster compaction stage and this step involves sorting of the processors based on the empty slots. Therefore, each pass through the compaction code is of the order of O(nis + p*log2p). In the worst case, p = nis. The number of required passes depends on the difference between AP and CNP and is given by the expression Q = log2(nis).Therefore, the complexity of compaction is O(nis2). The calculation of the utilization factor values involves the traversal of all the invocations of each subtask in the input graph. The complexity of this step is of the order of O(nis). Hence, the overall complexity is given by O(nis2+ e + e + nis2 + nis2 + nis ). For dense graphs, e is of the order of nis2. Hence, the time complexity for the specific DAG with nis tasks can be approximated as O(nis2). Therefore, the complexity for all hard real-time tasks would be = (n1s)2 + (n2s)2 + (n3s)2 + …….+ (nxs)2, where x is the total number of hard real-time DAGs in the application. div.head: 2) complexity due to hard subtasks:
div.p: The complexity analysis for the hard subtasks will be similar in many ways to the complexity analysis of the soft subtasks shown above. First, we need to calculate the complexity of one specific DAG dih that has nih subtasks. From the above analysis, we can conclude that this complexity will be O((nih)2). Now, DAG d1h will be run pp/pd1 times, DAG d2h will be run pp/pd2 times and so on. Hence, the complexity for all the hard subtasks will be: (n1h)2 * pp/pd1 + (n2h)2 *pp/pd2 + …. + (nyh)2 *pp/pdy, where y is the total number of soft real-time DAGs in the application. This equation can also be written as: pp*((n1h)2/pd1 + (n2h)2/pd2 + .... + (nyh)2/pdy) y = pp * (n i h )2/pd i j = 1 On adding the complexities of the soft and hard subtasks, we get the expression for the complexity of the proposed algorithm:

div.head: B. Space complexity:
div.p: The worst case space complexity of IDSA algorithm is of the order of (Nh)2 + (Ns)2, where Nh = pp*(1/pd1 + 1/pd2 + 1/pd3 + …. + 1/pdn), pp being the hyper period of the realtime application; pd1, pd2 etc. being the periods of the realtime tasks and Ns being the total number of soft tasks in the real-time application.

div.head: 1) Complexity due to hard tasks:
div.p: Each real-time subtask can be represented as a floating point and can therefore be stored in one memory cell. The total number of real-time tasks depends on the periods of the various tasks and can be given by hp/pd1 + hp/pd2 + hp/pd3 + ….+ hp/pdn = hp*(1/pd1 + 1/pd2 + 1/pd3 + …. + 1/pdn). For the sake of brevity, let's assume that this is equal to Nh. since each subtask needs one memory cell, Nh subtasks need x memory cells. For all DAGs, the total number of edges can be given by E. For very dense graphs, E = Nh2. Hence, all edges need Nh2 memory locations. The execution cost array for a subtask depends on the number of processors. If there are 4 available processors, then the execution cost array for each subtask will have 4 elements. Each subtask needs AP elements. Therefore, all Nh subtasks will need Nh*AP elements. Even though AP will be significantly lesser than Nh, in the worst case, there will be one subtask and one processor, so AP = Nh. Hence, all Nh subtasks will need Nh2 elements/memory locations. From Theorem S-3, it is clear that if the total number of subtasks = Nh, then in the worst case Nh -log2(1+Nh) subtasks need to be duplicated. For very large Nh, the 1 can be ignored, so we get Nh -log2(Nh). Again, for very large Nh, the term log2(Nh) can also be ignored (for example if Nh = 1024, then log2(1024) = 10 so the 10 can be ignored with respect to the 1024). Therefore, the number of subtasks that need to be duplicated = Nh. On adding all the above, we get Nh + Nh2 + Nh2 + Nh. Hence, the space complexity due to hard tasks is of the order of Nh2.

div.head: 2) Complexity due to soft tasks:
div.p: A logic similar to the one applied above can be applied to the soft tasks. Hence, the space complexity due to the soft tasks is of the order of Ns2, Ns being the total number of soft tasks in the real-time application. On combining the above two results, the space complexity of IDSA is of the order of Nh2 + Ns2.

div.head: C. Schedulability Condition 1:
div.p: A ti T is schedulable with IDSA, if the following condition is satisfied: ect(st(i,j,k) pp such that |succ(st(i,j,k)| = 0. The exit node is guaranteed to have zero successors. Because of the precedence constraints, the exit node will always be the last node to execute. A task set T = {t1, t2, t3, …., tap} will be schedulable with IDSA if the above test condition holds for all ti T. Note that the constituents of task set T can be hard tasks or soft tasks.

div.head: D. Schedulability Condition 2:
div.p: If UFhetero corresponds to the task load of the heterogeneous system, hetero corresponds to the communication load due to the hard subtask, hetero stands for the communication load for the soft subtasks, hetero stands for the idle load due to the hard tasks and hetero is the idle load due to the soft tasks, then a task set is schedulable with RT-DBA if: UFhetero AP -( hetero + hetero + hetero + hetero).

1) Calculating the communication load for the hard tasks: CL hetero refers to the communication load of the real-time application. The communication cost is the delay associated with the hard tasks data transmission and is given by c(h(i,j,k), h(i,l,k)) where h(i,j,k) and h(i,l,k) are the two communicating hard subtasks. Note that based on our model, subtasks that are part of the same task can communicate with each other (hence, the i term in both subtasks is the same). Also, data transmission is done between the same invocations of two communicating subtasks (hence, the k term in both subtasks is the same). The sum total of communication edge costs for all such pairs would give us the total communication cost for all hard tasks. Let's say that this cost = hetero . Hence, we get: hetero = c(h(i,j,k), h(i,l,k)) for all h i ∈ H and all ST(h i )

2) Calculating the communication load for the soft tasks: CL hetero refers to the communication load of the real-time application. The communication cost is the delay associated with the hard tasks data transmission and is given by c(s(i,j,k), s(i,l,k)) where s(i,j,k) and s(i,l,k) are the two communicating soft subtasks. Note that based on our model, subtasks that are part of the same task can communicate with each other (hence, the ith term in both subtasks is the same). Also, data transmission is done between the same invocations of two communicating subtasks (hence, the k term in both subtasks is the same). Let us define to be the set of all precedence related subtask pairs that are not assigned to the same processor. = {(s(i,j,k), s(i,l,k)} for all s i ∈ S where i, j, k and l are all integers. The sum total of communication edge costs for all such pairs would give us the total communication cost for all hard tasks. Let's say that this cost = hetero . Hence, we get: hetero = c(s(i,j,k), s(i,l,k)) for all s i ∈ S and all ST(s i )

3) Calculating the idle cost for hard tasks: Since IDSA is non-preemptive, there is a certain amount of time that a processor can be idle. Assume that there are two kids of cluster sets: the set for hard tasks, cl h and the set for soft tasks, cl s such that cl h = {cl h A real-time application will be schedulable if the sum of the task load, communication delay and idle time is less than the total processing capacity of the workstations. The total processing capacity = AP. Hence, we get, UFhetero + hetero + hetero + hetero + hetero AP. Hence, UFhetero AP -( hetero + hetero + hetero + hetero).

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, a duplication based scheduling algorithm for hard and soft tasks on a heterogeneous network of workstations has been proposed. Subtask duplication ensures that subtasks start and hence, finish earlier. Hence, a larger number of tasks are able to meet their deadlines. A detailed theoretical analysis of the proposed scheme has been done. In particular, the time and space complexity has been proved. Also, the schedulability conditions for ensuring that all deadlines are met have been derived. In the future work, this scheme is going to be tested using some popular real-time scheduling simulators such as LITMUS or RT-SIM.
